subject: Business Models
title: Shareware: The Predecessor
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Shareware: The Predecessor.

hook.text: In 1982, Andrew Fluegelman released a program called PC-Talk for free. He asked users to pay $25 if they liked it.

buildup.text: Shareware spread through floppy disks and BBSes. Try it free, pay the 'honor system' price later.

discovery.text: DOOM made shareware legendary. The first episode was free. Millions played it, thousands paid for the rest.

twist.text: Only 1-5% of shareware users ever paid. The model worked on volume, not conversion rate.

climax.text: Shareware proved free distribution could build massive audiences. It was freemium before the internet.

punchline.text: Floppy disks, honor system, 1% paid. Shareware invented freemium in 1982.

quiz.question: What was the typical payment rate for shareware?

details.summary: Shareware was the 1980s and 1990s predecessor to freemium, where developers distributed trial versions of software for free on floppy disks and bulletin boards, asking users to pay if they found it valuable. DOOM, WinZip, and WinRAR all used this honor-based distribution model.
details.whyItMatters: Shareware established the foundational principle that free distribution drives adoption, which freemium would later refine. It proved that letting users try before buying was more effective than traditional sales, even when most users never paid.
takeaways: Shareware distributed trial software freely, relying on voluntary payment
Floppy disk and BBS distribution enabled pre-internet viral spread
Most users never paid, but volume made the model viable for top products

faq.question: How did shareware distribution work before the internet?
faq.answer: Developers distributed software on floppy disks through computer magazines, user groups, and bulletin board systems. Users were encouraged to copy and share disks with friends. A nag screen reminded users to pay the registration fee, typically $20-50, to unlock the full version.

faq.question: What percentage of shareware users actually paid for the software?
faq.answer: Estimates suggest only 1-5% of shareware users paid the registration fee. Despite this, successful shareware like DOOM reached millions of users, making even 1% conversion enormously profitable. This conversion math later became the foundation of freemium financial models.
